summary: This informational memo documents how IPv4 is supported on MAPOS version 1.

eli5.summary: The recipe for sending ordinary Internet packets over this fiber system.

questions: how does ip run over mapos
subtitle: How to carry IP datagrams in MAPOS frames and how nodes find each other's 8-bit link addresses.

tldr.problem: MAPOS version 1 is a link layer that lets many nodes share SONET/SDH links through a frame switch, and IPv4 needs a defined way to ride on it and to map IP addresses to the 8-bit HDLC addresses.
tldr.mechanism: IP datagrams go in the information field of a MAPOS HDLC frame with protocol value 0x0021, and an Ethernet-like ARP with its own frame type, an UNARP message and cache rules maps IP addresses to HDLC addresses.
tldr.outcome: A short Informational memo, not a standard. It has since been updated by RFC 5494.

today: RFC 2176 is an Informational RFC and has been updated by RFC 5494. It documents how IPv4 is supported on MAPOS version 1 and was never a standards track document.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2176 describes how to send IPv4 over version 1 of MAPOS, the Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH defined in RFC 2171. MAPOS is a high-speed link layer protocol whose frames are based on the HDLC-like framing for PPP of RFC 1662. A component called a frame switch connects nodes in a star topology to form a LAN, which can span a wide area over long-haul SONET/SDH links.

The memo covers two things: how an IP datagram is encapsulated in a MAPOS HDLC frame, and how ARP maps between IP addresses and HDLC addresses. The authors note it is not the product of an IETF working group and has not necessarily had the in-depth review standards track documents receive.
sections.eli5: Many computers plug into one central box with fiber cables, like a group of friends all connected to one switchboard. This memo says how to send Internet messages through that switchboard.

sections.title: Encapsulating IP Datagrams
sections.content:
An IP datagram travels in a MAPOS HDLC frame. The frame's protocol field must contain 0x0021, as set out in the MAPOS Version 1 Assigned Numbers (RFC 2172), and the information field holds the datagram.

The information field may be one to 65,280 octets long, and that is the MTU of MAPOS. A large MTU reduces the overhead of IP header processing but may cause fragmentation anywhere along the path, hurting performance. To cope, Path MTU discovery (RFC 1191) may be used.
sections.eli5: The IP packet goes in an envelope with a tag saying 'this holds an Internet packet'. The envelope can be very big, but if a big one has to be cut up along the way, that can slow things down.

sections.title: MAPOS ARP
sections.content:
Before sending a datagram, a node must know the destination's HDLC address. MAPOS ARP is similar to Ethernet's. If the ARP cache has no entry, the node broadcasts an ARP request containing the destination IP address, and the node that owns that address replies with its HDLC address, which is then cached.

ARP frames use protocol field 0xFE01. The ARP packet's hardware address space is 25 (MAPOS, as assigned by IANA) and its protocol address space is 2048 for IP. Both address lengths are 4, and the operation code is 1 for a request and 2 for a response. Each hardware address occupies a 32-bit field with the 8-bit HDLC address in the least significant place and the remaining bits should be zero.

In a request, the sender fields hold the requester's addresses and the target HDLC address is all zeros because it is unknown. In a response the sender fields carry the replying node's addresses and the target fields carry the requester's.
sections.eli5: To send a letter you need the mailbox number. A computer shouts 'who has this Internet address?' and the owner answers 'that is me, my mailbox number is this one.' The answer is written down for next time.

sections.title: UNARP and ARP Cache Validation
sections.content:
Each node keeps an ARP cache of IP-to-HDLC mappings. Entries can be added manually or by ARP, and removed manually, by UNARP, or by cache validation. An implementation must let an operator add and remove arbitrary entries.

An implementation MUST provide UNARP, similar to the extension in RFC 1868. When a node detects that its port has come up, it MUST broadcast an UNARP packet, so every other node clears any stale entry left by whatever was previously connected to that switch port. UNARP is an ARP packet with operation code 23, the node's own addresses as sender, an all-ones target HDLC address and target IP address 255.255.255.255. The node MUST send three UNARP packets at 30 second intervals. A receiver MUST clear the entry for the sender's IP address if and only if the cached HDLC address differs from the one in the packet.

An implementation MUST also remove out-of-date entries and SHOULD allow the timeout to be configured, as RFC 1122 suggests. One approach is periodic timeouts even for entries in use, on the order of a minute or less. When the link is lost on an interface, for example by loss of carrier or loss of synchronization, all entries for that interface MUST be removed immediately.
sections.eli5: If someone new plugs into a plug that an old friend used, everyone's address book is wrong. The newcomer shouts 'forget the old number for this address' three times, half a minute apart, so everybody erases it.

sections.title: Broadcast and Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
In broadcast and multicast frames the most significant bit of the HDLC address must be 1. The least significant bit must always be 1 as well, to mark the end of the address field.

An IP broadcast maps to the HDLC broadcast address 0xFF, so the remaining six bits are all ones. For IP multicast, the remaining six bits carry the lowest-order six bits of the IP multicast group address, in the way RFC 1112 does for Ethernet. If those six bits are all zeros or all ones they should be changed to 111110.
sections.eli5: Some addresses mean 'everyone' or 'a group'. They are marked with special first and last bits, and a group's number is built from a small piece of the group's Internet address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo's security section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. It therefore gives no guidance on, for example, how a node should treat ARP or UNARP packets it cannot trust, even though UNARP makes receivers delete cache entries.
sections.eli5: The memo does not say anything about keeping this safe from troublemakers, so that part is left for the reader to think about.
